# Spec Build Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

Brings the project's compiled spec up to date, so what the harness reads of the spec is what the spec says now.

### Shape

#### Description

`piton build` runs in the project directory, compiling the spec and writing it out for the agents, the reference folder the harness reads included. A build runs either on its own, from a command, or ahead of other work that relies on the compiled spec.
Each build also writes the project's Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, to the fluency file in the project's data, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, whether the build succeeds or not, so the file keeps in step with the project's piton. Where the fluency can't be printed, the file is left as it was.

#### Owned Reference

The compiled reference, each reference folder the build writes for the project's adapters, as `.claude/reference`, is the build's own output, and nothing else's, so a file there the build's manifest doesn't list never stops a build the application runs, as where a project's manifest was lost, never made, or not kept with it, or a build elsewhere wrote the file. Where a build fails, and every error it reports is an `unowned-output` for a file inside a reference folder, the application deletes those files, and only those, and runs the build once more, straight away, as part of the same build: what that second build reports is how the build went, and the first one's errors are never shown as a failure. The work or notification it belongs to notes, as a passive line, never an error, how many reference files were replaced, as "Replaced 3 reference files the build didn't own".
A file outside the reference folders, as an instruction file in the code location, is never deleted, whatever the build says of it, since it may be the user's own: a build whose errors include an `unowned-output` for one fails as ever, with what it reported, and is not run again.

#### On Its Own

The Build Spec command, and Build in the palette, run a build on their own. They are unavailable while no project is open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, and while such a build is running, when the command shows a spinner and its tooltip says the spec is building. The build is listed among the [RunningActivityScope](../running-activity/index.md#running-activity-scope) as "Building the spec".
When the build is over, a notification says how it went. A build that succeeds is titled "Built 1 file" or "Built N files", and lists each file written on a line of its own, never wrapped. A build that fails is titled "Build failed", with what the build reported. When `piton build` can't be run at all, the notification is titled "Could not run piton build", with why.

#### Projects

A build run on its own belongs to the project it started in, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, and carries on when switching to another project. The command shows it running only while that project is on screen; another project can build at the same time. When it is over while another project is on screen, its notification's title ends with the name of the project it built, such as "Built 3 files in my-project".

#### Ahead Of Work

A build ahead of other work runs when that work actually starts, not when it is asked for, and shows as a step of that work until it is over. It isn't listed among the running activity on its own, since the work it leads is.
A build that fails, or can't be run, never stops the work that follows, since that work may be what fixes the spec, or can go on with the compiled spec as it was. The work says the build failed, so the compiled spec may be out of date, with what the build reported.

#### After Spec Work

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up, runs in a container with no code location, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, so any build it runs there writes only the reference it can see. Once its run is over, however it ended, done, failed, or cancelled, a build runs on the host, as one ahead of work does, so the host's compiled reference, and the shape guidance written into the code location, are those of the spec as the run left it. It runs before the task shows as finished, the task showing "Building" meanwhile, and then the task finishes in the state its run ended in. A build that fails, or can't be run, never changes that state: the task's output ends with a passive notice saying the build failed, with what it reported. The chain's next step is sent only once it is over.
Where that build fails because of the spec itself, that is, with any error but one it can't be run for, or an `unowned-output` it clears as Owned Reference says, the spec is fixed before anything goes on. Once the task finishes, a spec fix is sent at the head of the spec lane, carrying on its conversation: a Spec task, run as any is, in a container, whose prompt says that the spec no longer builds, and asks for it to be fixed, changing nothing else, followed by what the build reported, as written. It is listed beneath the task it fixes, as a chain's steps are, labelled "Spec fix" in Spec's colour, and a chain's next step waits for it, sent only once it is over. A spec fix is sent at most once for each task, never for a spec fix itself, so a build that still fails after it fails as ever, its passive notice saying so. A task that was cancelled, or failed, is never followed by a spec fix: its build fails as ever.
